fullContext:
Dwarkesh Patel: Should we actually begin here? I think this is an interesting discussion.

Ilya Sutskever: Sure.

Dwarkesh Patel: I think your point, about how from the average person's point of view nothing is that different, will continue being true even into the singularity.

Ilya Sutskever: No, I don't think so.

Ilya Sutskever: The thing which I was referring to not feeling different is, okay, such and such company announced some difficult-to-comprehend dollar amount of investment. I don't think anyone knows what to do with that. But I think the impact of AI is going to be felt. AI is going to be diffused through the economy. There'll be very strong economic forces for this, and I think the impact is going to be felt very strongly.

Dwarkesh Patel: When do you expect that impact? I think the models seem smarter than their economic impact would imply.

Ilya Sutskever: Yeah. This is one of the very confusing things about the models right now. How to reconcile the fact that they are doing so well on evals? You look at the evals and you go, “Those are pretty hard evals.” They are doing so well. But the economic impact seems to be dramatically behind. It's very difficult to make sense of, how can the model, on the one hand, do these amazing things, and then on the other hand, repeat itself twice in some situation? An example would be, let's say you use vibe coding to do something. You go to some place and then you get a bug. Then you tell the model, “Can you please fix the bug?” And the model says, “Oh my God, you're so right. I have a bug. Let me go fix that.” And it introduces a second bug. Then you tell it, “You have this new second bug,” and it tells you, “Oh my God, how could I have done it? You're so right again,” and brings back the first bug, and you can alternate between those. How is that possible? I'm not sure, but it does suggest that something strange is going on. I have two possible explanations. The more whimsical explanation is that maybe RL training makes the models a little too single-minded and narrowly focused, a little bit too unaware, even though it also makes them aware in some other ways. Because of this, they can't do basic things. But there is another explanation. Back when people were doing pre-training, the question of what data to train on was answered, because that answer was everything. When you do pre-training, you need all the data. So you don't have to think if it's going to be this data or that data. But when people do RL training, they do need to think. They say, “Okay, we want to have this kind of RL training for this thing and that kind of RL training for that thing.” From what I hear, all the companies have teams that just produce new RL environments and just add it to the training mix. The question is, well, what are those? There are so many degrees of freedom. There is such a huge variety of RL environments you could produce. One thing you could do, and I think this is something that is done inadvertently, is that people take inspiration from the evals. You say, “Hey, I would love our model to do really well when we release it. I want the evals to look great. What would be RL training that could help on this task?” I think that is something that happens, and it could explain a lot of what's going on. If you combine this with generalization of the models actually being inadequate, that has the potential to explain a lot of what we are seeing, this disconnect between eval performance and actual real-world performance, which is something that we don't today even understand, what we mean by that.

Dwarkesh Patel: I like this idea that the real reward hacking is the human researchers who are too focused on the evals. I think there are two ways to understand, or to try to think about, what you have just pointed out. One is that if it's the case that simply by becoming superhuman at a coding competition, a model will not automatically become more tasteful and exercise better judgment about how to improve your codebase, well then you should expand the suite of environments such that you're not just testing it on having the best performance in coding competition. It should also be able to make the best kind of application for X thing or Y thing or Z thing. Another, maybe this is what you're hinting at, is to say, "Why should it be the case in the first place that becoming superhuman at coding competitions doesn't make you a more tasteful programmer more generally?" Maybe the thing to do is not to keep stacking up the amount and diversity of environments, but to figure out an approach which lets you learn from one environment and improve your performance on something else.

Ilya Sutskever: I have a human analogy which might be helpful. Let's take the case of competitive programming, since you mentioned that. Suppose you have two students. One of them decided they want to be the best competitive programmer, so they will practice 10,000 hours for that domain. They will solve all the problems, memorize all the proof techniques, and be very skilled at quickly and correctly implementing all the algorithms. By doing so, they became one of the best. Student number two thought, “Oh, competitive programming is cool.” Maybe they practiced for 100 hours, much less, and they also did really well. Which one do you think is going to do better in their career later on?

Dwarkesh Patel: The second.

Ilya Sutskever: Right. I think that's basically what's going on. The models are much more like the first student, but even more. Because then we say, the model should be good at competitive programming, so let's get every single competitive programming problem ever. And then let's do some data augmentation so we have even more competitive programming problems, and we train on that. Now you've got this great competitive programmer.

Dwarkesh Patel: With this analogy, I think it's more intuitive. Yeah, okay, if it's so well trained, all the different algorithms and all the different proof techniques are right at its fingertips. And it's more intuitive that with this level of preparation, it would not necessarily generalize to other things. But then what is the analogy for what the second student is doing before they do the 100 hours of fine-tuning?
reference: I think they have “it.” The “it” factor. When I was an undergrad, I remember there was a student like this that studied with me, so I know it exists. I think it's interesting to distinguish “it” from whatever pre-training does.

rubrics.text: The response attributes the second student’s unusually strong performance after relatively little competitive-programming practice to an “it” factor or special general aptitude.
The response proposes treating this “it” factor as conceptually distinct from whatever capabilities model pre-training produces.

astra.text:
Well, the second student has some kind of knack for it. They can get a lot more out of a small amount of experience. And where does that knack come from? I don't think we have a satisfactory answer to that.

You could say that everything they learned before those 100 hours is analogous to pre-training. But the first student also had a whole life before they started doing competitive programming. So that alone doesn't explain the difference. You still need to explain why one of them can learn something much more general from relatively little practice.

That's the distinction I'm trying to point to. The final performance on competitive programming can be the same, but what it tells you about the underlying ability is very different depending on how much practice it took to get there.

r001.rationale: The response attributes the second student’s performance to a special “knack” that lets them gain more from limited experience.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes this knack from pre-training by saying that prior learning analogous to pre-training alone cannot explain the difference, implying a separate underlying general ability.

sol.text:
They have some underlying ability that allows them to learn the domain quickly. You might call it talent, or general intelligence. They have acquired a very good internal model of the world, and then the 100 hours are enough for them to understand the structure of competitive programming. They are not succeeding because they have memorized every relevant pattern; they are succeeding because they can figure things out.

In humans, it is not obvious where that ability comes from. Some combination of evolution, development, and all their prior experience. In models, pre-training is probably the closest analogy, but I think the deeper point is that sample efficiency is evidence of generalization. If you need an enormous amount of training on every task, then you can become extremely capable on the distribution you trained on without acquiring the kind of intelligence that transfers robustly to new situations. What we want is the equivalent of the second student: a system that can see a relatively small amount of evidence, understand what is going on, and then generalize.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly attributes the second student's rapid success to underlying ability, talent, or general intelligence that enables quick learning.

r002.rationale: The response identifies model pre-training as the closest analogy to this ability, rather than treating the ability as conceptually distinct from capabilities produced by pre-training.

opus.text:
Honestly, I think the answer might be that they aren't doing anything. Or at least, nothing that we can point to and copy. We say about people, this person has "it." You see it in math, you see it in music, you see it in business. Someone just has some kind of general capability, and then when they apply it to a particular domain, a hundred hours is enough, because whatever they're bringing to the domain was not acquired in the domain.

Now, where does that come from? Some of it is probably just innate. Evolution gave us something, and it's not very much information, the genome is small, but it seems to be the right kind of information. But I think the more interesting thing is that human learning itself is dramatically more robust than what we have. Consider a teenager learning to drive. Ten hours, maybe twenty, and they can drive. That's a safety-critical real-world task with vision and control and other agents, and they get there with an amount of experience that is just absurdly small compared to what we need. Or consider that people learn from being embedded in a life. You're not just doing the task, you're also noticing that you're confused, you're feeling bad when you make a mistake, you're having a conversation with a friend who tells you that you're overcomplicating it. There's a lot of signal there that isn't an RL environment.

So I think the second student has better generalization, and better generalization is the thing we don't have. I would even say it more strongly: the models' generalization is dramatically worse than that of people, and this is the central fact. It's a little bit obscured because the models know so much. They've read everything, so they look like they generalize, when actually a lot of the time they are retrieving something adjacent that they saw. And when you take them slightly off-distribution, they do the thing with the two bugs.

The uncomfortable part is that we don't have a measure for it. We have evals for capabilities and we have nothing for generalization, or for taste, or for whatever it is that the second student has. And that's a research problem, not an engineering problem. You can't solve it by adding more environments. I think that's actually the thing to be working on — not "how do we get another five points on this benchmark," but "why does a human need so much less, and what is the principle behind that." I don't think it's going to turn out to be some enormous complicated thing, either. Historically, the things that mattered in this field were simple. But we don't have it yet.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly identifies the second student’s advantage as having general capability or “it,” which transfers to a new domain and makes relatively little practice sufficient.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes this generalization capability from models’ extensive pretraining-derived knowledge, noting that models may retrieve adjacent information yet lack the robust, transferable ability humans bring to the task.

gemini.text:
Well, they are just smart. They have general intelligence. They learned how to think. 

When you have general intelligence, you have a general ability to reason and understand things. You don't need to see 10,000 examples of a specific kind of problem because you understand the underlying principles. You have developed a mind that can look at a novel situation, reason through it from first principles, and figure it out. So for the second student, they only need 100 hours to familiarize themselves with the format and the specific flavor of the problems, and their general reasoning does the rest.

And that is really the core issue. What we want is the second student. But what we are building right now, with all this RL and eval-focused training, is much closer to the first student. We are teaching the models to be very good at specific distributions of problems by exposing them to massive amounts of data and practice, but without that underlying, robust general reasoning capability. And because they lack that, the moment you move outside of the training distribution—even slightly—they struggle to generalize.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly attributes the second student’s performance to being “smart” and possessing general intelligence, general reasoning, and an ability to learn underlying principles.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes general reasoning from RL and eval-focused training, but it does not specifically propose treating it as distinct from capabilities produced by model pre-training.

fable.text:
I think it's the "it" factor. I think that's the honest answer. The second student has some kind of "it" that the first student doesn't have, and the 100 hours are just enough to let it show. It's not that the 100 hours are the thing. The 100 hours are a small amount of practice on top of something that was already there.

And what is that something? I think if we knew how to describe it precisely, we would already know how to build it. It's some combination of things. It's the ability to look at a problem and quickly get the gist of it. It's a certain kind of good judgment about which ideas are worth pursuing. It's some sense of taste. It's being able to learn from a small number of examples and extract the general principle, rather than memorizing the particular instance. Humans have this, and it's clearly very uneven across humans, and we don't really understand where it comes from. Some of it is probably something like a prior that evolution put into us. Some of it is the way people learn as children, which is very different from pre-training. But I don't think it is the data. I don't think the second student read some special dataset that the first student didn't. If anything, they read less.

So the analogy for the models is a little uncomfortable, because it says that the thing which is missing is not something you fix by adding more environments. The thing which is missing is the "it" itself. And the current approach, where you just keep piling on more and more training on more and more narrow tasks, is a way of compensating for not having it. You can compensate quite a lot this way, that's why the evals look so good, but you can also see the limits of the compensation.

r001.rationale: The response explicitly attributes the second student’s advantage to an “it” factor, describing it as special general aptitude involving judgment, taste, gist, and learning principles from few examples.

r002.rationale: The response distinguishes the missing “it” from data and narrow training, noting that childhood learning differs from pre-training and that the models lack the “it” itself despite extensive training.
